Here is a concise, targeted extraction based on the dataset page:

Direct CSV/TSV download URL
- sound_heat_flux.csv (CSV) is provided as a downloadable data file within the Dryad dataset. The page lists this file as part of the dataset contents; click through to download sound_heat_flux.csv from the dataset’s file list.
- Note: The page itself does not display a direct HTTP link to the CSV/TSV; you’ll obtain the exact download URL by opening the dataset page and selecting the sound_heat_flux.csv file in the Files section.

What each column measures (sound_heat_flux.csv)
- time: Time stamp corresponding to the hydrophone acoustic reading (seconds).
- sound: Acoustic signal reading from the hydrophone (arbitrary units, a.u.).
- Time (s): Interpolated time marks corresponding to the calculated heat flux (seconds).
- heat flux: Interpolated heat flux value (units: W/cm^2) derived from linear regression of temperature profiles.
- r: Row number index within the spreadsheet.

Sample size
- The dataset description mentions a 9.60 GB file bundle (ned3-004_BoilingAcousticsHydrophone.zip) containing raw acoustic data and related files. The exact number of rows in sound_heat_flux.csv is not stated on the page; you would need to inspect the CSV header or sample rows within the file to determine N (the number of samples). The accompanying Boiling-32_Temperature.lvm and Boiling-32_Hydrophone.lvm indicate multi-sensor recordings, but an explicit sample count is not provided in the highlights.

Headline finding (effect size, p-value)
- The highlights describe a machine learning study mapping acoustic signals to heat flux during pool boiling and identify:
  - The fast Fourier transform – Gaussian process regression (FFT-GPR) combination as the most promising model with high accuracy and low computational cost.
  - Acoustic features below 512 Hz are most significant for heat flux predictions.
  - For sampling rates above 512 Hz, performance is governed by the temporal length of acoustic sequences.
- There is no statistical test result reported in the dataset highlights (no p-values or explicit effect sizes for the heat flux predictions). Hence, no effect size or p-value is provided in the available materials. The emphasis is on model performance (accuracy and computational cost) rather than hypothesis testing statistics.

If you want, I can guide you through extracting the exact number of samples from sound_heat_flux.csv and, if present, any accompanying performance metrics (e.g., RMSE, R^2) from readme or related documentation.
